cards.explanation: The answer is that he offers sacrifices to God. At Beersheba he offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. The text puts those sacrifices right there on the way out of Canaan. I'd have stopped to check whether I left the oven on, so I'm glad this stop was about God.

The answer is nation. God says, “…I will make you into a great nation there.” Think about that for a second, friends. It's one old man with his family on the road, and God calls him a future nation. That's a big promise from the One who makes it.
The answer is True. God tells Jacob, “I will go down with you to Egypt…” Jacob isn't headed down there on his own. He has family around him, and he has God's word that God goes with him.

The answer is that God will bring him back. God says, “…I will surely bring you back.” He doesn't just promise to go down there with Jacob. He promises to bring him back, and that word "surely" is a strong one.

The answer is False. The text says they took the livestock and the possessions they had acquired in Canaan, and Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt. Nobody left the flocks at home. That's a lot of moving for one trip.

The answer is Judah. Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen (Genesis 46:28). Jacob has one of his sons go first and find the way. I'd make a terrible scout, since I can get turned around between the oven and the counter.

The answer is False. Joseph prepared his chariot and went to meet his father, and then the text says he presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely (Genesis 46:29). So he doesn't greet his father from up high. He holds him and cries hard. Jacob once believed Joseph was gone (Genesis 37:33–35), so I think this hug carries a whole lot of feeling.

The answer is that he has seen Joseph is still alive. Israel says, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” His reason is right there in his own words: he has seen Joseph's face, and he knows Joseph is alive. I think that moment hits him all at once.

The answer is True. Joseph tells the brothers to say they have raised livestock since they were young, and that their fathers did too. It's a true answer, because shepherds are exactly what they are. Joseph is coaching them to say what's real.

The answer is that Egyptians detest all shepherds. Joseph says they'll be allowed to settle in Goshen, “…since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.” So the brothers say they're shepherds, plain and honest. The very thing the Egyptians dislike gets them a place of their own.

The answer is that there's no pasture for their flocks. They tell Pharaoh, “…there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe.” Flocks are what they raise, and the famine is the reason they give. They keep it plain and don't dress it up.
The answer is False. Pharaoh says, “settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land.” They get the best, not the leftovers. The king is generous here, friends.

The answer is livestock. Pharaoh says, “And if you know of any talented men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock.” Notice it starts with “if.” It's an offer, and Pharaoh doesn't say such men are there. He just says what the job would be.

The answer is True. Joseph brings in his father Jacob and presents him before Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and Jacob blesses him (Genesis 47:7). Then verse 10 says Jacob blessed Pharaoh again as he departed. So Jacob blesses him at both ends of the visit. That's a good way to walk into a room and a good way to walk out.
The answer is 130. Jacob says, “My travels have lasted 130 years…” Notice he calls them his travels. That's how he describes a long life on the road.
The answer is few and hard. Jacob says, “My years have been few and hard…” That's an honest answer, and I think a tender one. He doesn't dress it up for the king.

The answer is food for their families. The text says Joseph provided his father and brothers and all his father's household with food for their families. Land is nice, but a family has to eat. Joseph makes sure that gets done.
